planting.note: Direct sow onto bare mineral soil in early spring as soon as it can be worked; in milder winters seed can be scattered in fall instead, mimicking the natural self-sowing cycle, since seedlings survive hard frost as small rosettes.

directions: Deerhorn clarkia is a slender, wiry-stemmed annual of the Columbia Basin's bunchgrass steppe and basalt scabland openings, named for its small four-petaled pink to lavender flowers, each petal pinched into a narrow claw with a dark central blotch. It germinates on open, disturbed, low-fertility soil and completes flowering and seed-set quickly before summer drought arrives, making it well suited to gravel beds, dryland meadow mixes, or bare patches left between rock-garden plantings. Rich soil or regular watering produces floppy growth and fewer blooms, so keep it lean and dry. Once seed has fallen on a compatible gritty site it will reseed itself for years.

planting.note: Plant dormant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in fall into very lean, sharply drained gravelly or rocky soil in full sun; do not irrigate in summer once the foliage has died back.

directions: Sagebrush mariposa lily sends up a single grass-like leaf and a wiry stem topped with large, long-lasting lavender-to-magenta cup flowers, each petal marked with a darker chevron and a dense fringe of hairs near the base. It grows wild on basalt scabland rims and gravelly steppe benches across the Columbia Basin, going summer-dormant soon after bloom in a pattern gardeners must respect by marking bulb locations and keeping the site bone-dry from midsummer on. It is best grown in a raised bed, rock garden, or bulb frame where winter and spring moisture is followed by reliable summer drought. Plants increase slowly from bulblets and resent any disturbance once settled.

planting.note: Fall-sow onto shallow, rocky or gravelly soil and let winter moisture and cold naturally break seed dormancy; established plants can also be set out from containers in spring.

directions: Thyme-leaf buckwheat forms a low, woody-based mat of narrow gray-green leaves rolled at the edges like true thyme, hugging the shallow soil pockets and crevices of basalt scablands and bunchgrass-steppe scree across the Columbia Basin. Rounded clusters of small white to pale pink flowers open on short stalks in early summer and age to rusty tones, drawing a steady traffic of native bees and small butterflies through the hottest part of the season. It needs sharply drained, mineral soil and almost no summer water, making it a strong candidate for rock gardens, gravel paths, and crevice plantings rather than irrigated beds. Avoid mulch or rich soil, both of which encourage rot at the woody crown.

planting.note: Sow fresh seed directly into its permanent spot in fall, since the thick taproot resists transplanting; expect erratic germination over one or two winters as natural cold-moist stratification breaks dormancy.

directions: Gray's desert parsley is a strongly aromatic, finely dissected perennial that roots directly into basalt talus and shallow scabland soil pockets across the Columbia Basin, often appearing on sites too rocky for almost anything else. Flat clusters of small yellow flowers open very early in spring, often among the first bloom on the scablands, feeding early-flying bees and serving as a larval host for Indra and Anise swallowtail butterflies. The crushed foliage has a pungent, celery-and-turpentine scent distinct among native parsleys, and the thick taproot stores reserves to carry the plant through long summer drought. Grow it in a lean rock garden or dry slope planting and never irrigate once established.

planting.note: Fall-sow onto open, gravelly soil so seedlings can form a low rosette before winter; plants overwinter as rosettes and bloom the following spring.

directions: Douglas' bladderpod forms a low rosette of silvery, hairy leaves close to the ground, from which short stalks of bright yellow four-petaled flowers emerge among the very earliest bloom on the Columbia Basin's basalt scablands, often flowering while nights are still freezing. The puffed, bladder-like seed pods that follow give the plant its common name and add interest after the flowers fade. It is short-lived, typically behaving as a winter annual or biennial, and thrives only in thin, mineral, fast-draining soil pockets with no competition from taller vegetation. Let it self-sow in a gravel bed or scree garden rather than trying to maintain it as a permanent clump.

planting.note: Nick or lightly sand the hard seed coat before fall sowing to speed germination, then sow directly into gritty, well-drained soil since the taproot dislikes transplanting.

directions: Woollypod milkvetch grows as a low, silvery-haired cushion of pinnate leaves tucked into gravelly scabland soil pockets and bunchgrass-steppe openings across the Columbia Basin, bearing clusters of pea-like purple-pink flowers close to the foliage in early spring. The common name comes from the distinctive seed pods that follow, each swollen into a densely woolly, balloon-like capsule that persists on the plant well after bloom. As a nitrogen-fixing legume it needs no supplemental fertility and actually performs worse in rich soil, while its early flowers provide an important nectar source for native bees before most steppe wildflowers have opened. Grow it in a lean rock garden or gravel bed with no summer irrigation.
